newsitem.title: USA: Aetna down after disappointing Q4 results.
newsitem.headline: Aetna down after disappointing Q4 results.

text.p: Shares of Aetna Inc fell about four percent in early afternoon trading after the company reported disappointing fourth quarter earnings, hurt by unfavorable pricing and higher medical costs, analysts said.
Aetna reported fourth quarter operating earnings of $0.81 a share compared with analysts' First Call consensus estimate of $0.85 a share. Aetna shares were down 3-3/8 to 79.
Aetna's medical cost loss ratio rose to 83.1 percent in the fourth quarter compared with expectations for 81.3 percent and with 78.0 percent a year ago, analysts said.
The disappointing earnings gave investor a reason to take profits following the stock's recent strong performance, industry sources said.
"Medical cost inflation was evident," Bear Stearns analyst Gary Frazier said.
Costs were up throughout the year because of depressed premium rate increases and rising medical costs, Salomon Brothers analyst Robert Hoehn said in a research report.
The most prominent elements of the rise in fourth quarter medical costs were the impact of mandatory 48-hour maternity stays and pharmacy costs, Hoehn said in the report.
The maternity stay factor has been in place for a year now and thus the year to year comparison in 1997 should not produce the same increase, he said.
Frazier said the results also were hurt by the pricing in Aetna's medical business, which was flat compared with last quarter and below analysts' expectations.
However, Frazier said Aetna expects an improved pricing environment in 1997.
Price increases of three to five percent are expected for HMO products, four to six percent for point-of-service, and seven to 12 percent on indemnity, Salomon's Hoehn said.

Aetna also told analysts it will not know the results of recontracting efforts with New York hospitals relative to the tax on health insurance and the deregulation of hospital rates until the end of the first quarter, Hoehn said in the report.
Meanwhile, growth in Aetna's international business also fell short of expectations, Oppenheimer analyst Lori Price said in a research report.
But the slower growth was attributable to the new investments the company is making in the emerging markets, she said in the report.
Aetna earlier this week said it will make an initial investment of $300 million to acquire up to 49 percent of a joint venture with Brazil's largest life insurance company.
The deal is expected to close in the second quarter and contribute to earnings by year end, Salomon's Hoehn said.
Although the deal adds momentum to the international business, Hoehn said it may disappoint investors who are hoping that Aetna will divest its non-U.S. health business.
